text: A Scheduled Analytics Rule's KQL query has to come from somewhere. Sentinel gives you two real starting points: a built-in rule template already written by Microsoft, or a custom rule you write entirely yourself. Which one fits depends on whether the thing you're watching for is a common, well-understood threat or something specific to your own environment, and most real deployments end up needing both.

Under Configuration, Analytics, Rule templates, there are hundreds of pre-built rules, organized by data source and MITRE ATT&CK tactic, each with its query, recommended schedule, severity, and entity mapping already filled in by Microsoft's own security research teams and updated over time as new templates ship. Most need only one thing from you: the matching data connector turned on, since a template built for one data source returns nothing without it feeding the workspace.

A custom rule starts from a blank query instead. You write the KQL, set the schedule, threshold, and entity mapping yourself, the same pieces covered elsewhere in this chapter, just authored from scratch. Custom rules are the only option for logic no vendor could anticipate — a custom app's own log table, or an org-specific business rule like after-hours access to a finance system by the wrong role.

Built-in rules give fast time-to-value and vetted logic with low maintenance, but they're tuned for the general case and sometimes noisy until adjusted. Custom rules give an exact fit for a scenario only your organization has, but every clause, and every future tuning pass, is work you own.

Neither approach wins outright. Most real Sentinel deployments run a mix: templates enabled for the broad, well-known threats across the environment, and a smaller set of custom rules covering the handful of things genuinely unique to that organization. Next, Lesson 11 covers entity mapping — how Sentinel turns a query's plain columns into entities it can actually track and correlate across incidents.
